explain: The brevity penalty equals 1 when the candidate is at least as long as the reference, and penalizes only shorter outputs, which could cheat on precision with a few correct words.
options: Penalizing candidates shorter than the reference, which would have inflated precision
Penalizing overly long and verbose candidates, which lower recall on the reference
Rewarding candidates with a broad and varied vocabulary, even if absent from the reference
Normalizing the score by the number of references available for each candidate sentence
q: What is the purpose of the brevity penalty in the BLEU metric?

explain: ROUGE is recall-oriented: it measures how much of the reference is captured by the generated summary, and it is the standard metric for summarization.
options: The precision of the candidate n-grams, measured exactly as the BLEU metric does in translation
The recall of n-grams, that is, how much of the reference is covered by the summary
The perplexity of the model on the summarized text, as in standard language modeling
The generation latency of the summary measured in tokens per second in production
q: Unlike BLEU, what is the ROUGE metric primarily oriented toward?

explain: ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence between candidate and reference, thus also capturing word order at the sentence level.
options: The uniform average of precision over unigrams and bigrams extracted from the candidate text
The count of skip-bigrams validated one by one by expert human evaluators
The longest common subsequence between candidate and reference, sensitive to order
The cross-entropy loss computed on the summarized text against the given reference
q: What is the ROUGE-L variant based on?

explain: Perplexity measures the model's uncertainty in predicting the next token: lower values indicate more confident and fluent predictions.
options: Higher is better, because a high value signals greater creativity and richness of the model
Higher is better, because it indicates that the model explores a broader vocabulary
It must always equal 1, the only value compatible with a well-trained model
Lower is better, because it indicates less uncertainty in predicting the next token
q: In language modeling, how is perplexity interpreted?

explain: Perplexity = exp of the average negative log-likelihood loss: if the loss drops with fine-tuning, perplexity drops too.
options: Perplexity decreases, because it is the exponential of the average loss on the test set
Perplexity increases, because after fine-tuning the model remains more surprised
Perplexity stays unchanged, because it does not depend on average loss in any way
Perplexity becomes negative, dropping below zero like the logarithmic loss
q: A model has an average negative log-likelihood loss of 2.7 on the test set; after fine-tuning the loss drops to 2.0. What happens to perplexity?

explain: Quantization represents weights and activations with fewer bits (from FP32 to FP16/INT8/FP8), reducing memory footprint and computational cost.
options: Increasing the number of model parameters to improve its expressive capacity
Representing weights and activations with fewer bits than FP32 precision
Removing entire layers from the model to reduce its depth and memory footprint
Training the model on multiple GPUs in parallel to speed up initial convergence
q: What does quantization do at the numerical representation level?

explain: PTQ converts an already trained model without retraining it, while QAT simulates the effects of quantization during training to better preserve accuracy.
options: PTQ always requires full retraining, while QAT never really requires it
PTQ only applies to FP16 precision and QAT only to INT8 precision on TPU
PTQ quantizes a trained model without retraining it, QAT simulates it during training
They are two different names for the same identical post-training compression technique
q: What is the difference between post-training quantization (PTQ) and quantization-aware training (QAT)?

explain: Pruning removes weights, neurons or channels deemed unimportant, making the model smaller and sparser.
options: Adding new layers to the model to increase its total representational capacity
Increasing weight precision by bringing them back from INT8 to FP32 on every single layer
Compressing the training dataset by removing examples deemed less informative
Removing unimportant weights, neurons or channels to make the model smaller
q: What does pruning do in a neural model?

explain: Structured pruning removes entire structures (channels, filters, layers) and is hardware-friendly; unstructured pruning removes individual weights, creating sparsity that requires specific hardware support.
options: Structured pruning removes entire channels and is hardware-friendly, unstructured pruning removes individual weights
There is no practical difference between the two approaches in terms of sparsity ever produced
Structured pruning always increases model size, while unstructured pruning reduces it
Unstructured pruning only applies to transformers and structured pruning only to convolutional networks
q: What is the difference between structured and unstructured pruning?

explain: In distillation, a small and fast student learns to imitate the output distributions (soft labels) of a large teacher, offering cheap inference with quality close to the teacher's.
options: A large model imitating a small model to increase its overall capacity
A small student model learning to imitate the predictions of a large teacher
A model progressively pruned after each single training epoch
A model whose weights are dynamically quantized at every batch during inference
q: In a teacher-student knowledge distillation setup, which statement is correct?

explain: Data drift is the change in the production data distribution relative to training; continuous monitoring serves to detect it before it degrades performance.
options: Increased response latency due to network congestion in production
Irreversible loss of model weights occurring after deployment to production
Change in the production data distribution compared to the training data
Increased storage costs from retaining historical inference logs
q: When monitoring an LLM in production, what is meant by data drift?

explain: Versioning models allows comparing versions with each other and quickly returning to a previous stable version in case of regressions.
options: To reduce model weight size with each new release put into production
To automatically increase model accuracy with each release without evaluating it
To avoid evaluation entirely, replaced by simply counting the releases produced
To track model versions to enable direct comparisons and fast rollbacks
q: Why is model versioning important in LLM deployment?

explain: BLEU and ROUGE measure lexical overlap with a reference and do not detect factual errors or hallucinations: human evaluation or specialized judges are needed for factual correctness.
options: Because metrics like BLEU and ROUGE do not detect factual errors and hallucinations
Because automatic metrics are too expensive to compute on large volumes
Because human evaluation always increases the BLEU score obtained no matter what
Because public benchmarks are forbidden in production evaluation pipelines
q: Why does human evaluation remain necessary even when using automatic metrics?

explain: METEOR extends BLEU by handling stemming, synonyms and better alignment, with higher correlation to human judgment than pure BLEU.
options: It only measures inference latency, completely ignoring text quality
It considers stemming, synonyms and alignment, correlating better with human judgment than BLEU
It always requires a human judge in the loop to evaluate every single sentence generated by the model
It only works for document retrieval and never evaluates machine translation
q: Which feature distinguishes the METEOR metric from BLEU?

explain: Exact match requires exact string identity and penalizes correct but paraphrased answers; for generative QA it is paired with token-level F1, which gives partial credit for overlap.
options: The system has completely failed, because an EM of 0 always indicates an unusable answer
EM must be abandoned and only perplexity used to evaluate every generated answer produced
EM is too rigid here: token-level F1 should complement it
The reference should be eliminated and any answer mentioning the word Paris accepted
q: A QA system generates 'Paris is the French capital' while the reference is 'Paris': the exact match is 0. What does an expert evaluator conclude?

explain: BLEU computes the modified precision of n-grams (how many candidate n-grams appear in the references, with clipped counts) and not recall.
options: The recall of reference n-grams, that is, how much is covered by the candidate
The average negative log-likelihood of the model on the parallel translation corpus
The semantic similarity between contextual embeddings of candidate and reference translated by the model
The modified precision of the candidate n-grams against the available references
q: What does BLEU fundamentally measure?

explain: BLEU ranges from 0 to 1 (often reported 0-100): 1 indicates a perfect match with the reference, 0 no overlap.
options: From 0 to 1 (or 0-100), where 1 indicates a perfect match with the reference
From -1 to 1, where 0 is the best possible result and 1 indicates total disagreement
From 0 to infinity, with no upper bound as matching n-grams grow
Always between 0 and 0.5 by mathematical construction, never reaching the maximum
q: What is the range of the BLEU score and how is the upper end interpreted?

explain: BLEU requires exact n-gram matches: a correct paraphrase with different words gets a low score, so it misses synonyms and paraphrases.
options: It tends to reward creative synonyms too much, always giving them excessive weight
It does not capture synonyms and paraphrases, because it requires exact n-gram matches
It always perfectly measures deep understanding of the text translated by the model
It is entirely independent of the reference length used for the final comparison
q: A candidate translates correctly but uses synonyms never present in the reference: which BLEU limitation emerges?

explain: ROUGE-N counts n-gram overlap of order N (ROUGE-1 unigrams, ROUGE-2 bigrams), while ROUGE-L evaluates the longest common subsequence, sensitive to order at the sentence level.
options: ROUGE-N measures text perplexity, while ROUGE-L measures its average latency
ROUGE-N and ROUGE-L are two different names given to the same identical basic mathematical formula
ROUGE-N measures n-gram overlap of order N, ROUGE-L uses the longest common subsequence
ROUGE-N only applies to machine translation and ROUGE-L only to textual retrieval
q: What is the difference between ROUGE-N and ROUGE-L?

explain: ROUGE-W weights the longest common subsequence giving more credit to consecutive matches, thus rewarding fluency and correct word order.
options: A variant computing overlap using only the candidate text stopwords
A compression metric measuring model weight reduction in memory
A perplexity variant designed specifically for very long texts
A variant weighting the longest common subsequence to reward consecutive matches
q: What characterizes the ROUGE-W variant?

explain: With imbalanced classes, accuracy is dominated by the majority class; a low F1 on the rare class reveals that the model almost entirely ignores it.
options: The model does well on the majority class but fails on the rare one: accuracy alone misleads
The model is excellent on all classes, because an accuracy of 0.90 guarantees high F1 everywhere
F1 is miscalculated, because with accuracy 0.90 it is impossible to get an F1 of 0.30
The model should be discarded for overfitting, because any gap between accuracy and F1 indicates overfitting
q: A model on imbalanced classes has accuracy 0.90 but F1 of 0.30 on the rare class. How is the result interpreted?

explain: Precision indicates, among elements predicted positive, how many are truly positive; recall indicates, among all real positives, how many were found.
options: They are two different names for the same identical quality measure of the classifier
Precision is measured on predicted positives, recall on all real positives
Precision counts true positives over all real positives, recall over predicted positives
Precision only applies to document retrieval, recall only to translation
q: In a classification task, what is the difference between precision and recall?

explain: With imbalanced classes, a trivial model that always predicts the majority class gets high accuracy but low F1 on the rare class: accuracy alone is misleading.
options: Accuracy is always the best metric to use in every possible scenario
With imbalanced classes F1 must be abandoned and only the BLEU metric used for everything
High accuracy with an always-majority predictor means nothing: precision, recall and F1 are needed
The confusion matrix is never useful and can be ignored entirely in these practical cases
q: A dataset has 95% negative examples. A model that always predicts negative gets accuracy 0.95. What does an experienced ML engineer conclude?

explain: The confusion matrix tabulates true/false positives and negatives, from which precision, recall, F1 and accuracy derive: it is the basic diagnostic tool.
options: The total number of model parameters represented in compact tabular form
The training loss curve plotted epoch by epoch during the entire training performed
The average inference time per batch measured on the production hardware used
True and false positive/negative counts used to derive precision, recall and F1
q: What does a confusion matrix show for a binary classifier?

explain: Macro-average averages per-class metrics giving equal weight to each class; micro-average aggregates all counts, giving more weight to frequent classes.
options: Macro-average weighs classes equally, micro-average aggregates counts and favors frequent ones
They are identical in all possible cases and always produce exactly the same value
Macro-average only applies to the BLEU metric and micro-average only to the ROUGE metric in practice
Micro-average always completely ignores the majority class present in the dataset
q: What is the difference between macro-average and micro-average of F1 in multiclass classification?

explain: Perplexity is monotonically linked to loss: going from 15 to 8 means much more confident predictions, a clear improvement in language modeling.
options: The model has worsened and is now much more uncertain in its final predictions
The model has clearly improved: it predicts test-set tokens with less uncertainty
Nothing relevant has changed, because perplexity does not measure real quality
The model now hallucinates more, because low perplexity always causes more hallucinations
q: An LLM perplexity on the test set goes from 15 to 8 after fine-tuning. How is the result interpreted?

explain: MRR rewards the rank of the first relevant result (1/rank), nDCG evaluates the graded quality of the whole list with logarithmic discount by position: they are the standard ranking metrics in retrieval.
options: The indexing time of documents in the collection used by the vector retrieval system
The total size of the vector index built with document embeddings
Ranking quality: MRR looks at the rank of the first relevant result, nDCG at the whole graded list
The perplexity of the retriever computed on documents retrieved for each query
q: In a RAG system, what do MRR and nDCG measure in the retrieval phase?

explain: The ROC curve relates true positive rate and false positive rate as the threshold varies; AUC (0.5 random, 1.0 perfect) summarizes the discriminative ability of the classifier.
options: The training loss plotted as a function of the number of training epochs performed
The BLEU score plotted as a function of the generated candidate text length
The inference latency plotted as a function of the batch size used in production in the test
True positive rate versus false positive rate across thresholds, summarized by AUC
q: What does an ROC curve and its AUC represent?

explain: BERTScore compares contextual token embeddings instead of exact n-grams, recognizing synonyms and paraphrases that BLEU would penalize.
options: BERTScore matches contextual embeddings, so it captures synonyms that BLEU misses
BLEU is a deep semantic metric while BERTScore remains only lexical and rigid by nature
They are both latency metrics and do not measure text quality in any way
BERTScore only measures text length without ever comparing it to the reference
q: Why is BERTScore often preferred over BLEU for evaluating semantic similarity between candidate and reference?

explain: In dynamic quantization, weights are statically quantized while activations are quantized on the fly at each inference, with no need for calibration data or retraining.
options: A technique that fully retrains the model at every single request received in production
Activations quantized on the fly during inference, without calibration or retraining
A type of dynamic pruning removing entire model layers during inference
A form of online distillation where teacher and student continuously update each other
q: What is meant by dynamic quantization?

explain: INT8 calibration uses a representative dataset to estimate activation scales and zero-points, so as to map the real dynamic range well and contain the accuracy drop.
options: Adjusting the learning rate automatically after each single training epoch
Precisely counting the total model parameters before the compression phase
Estimating activation scales and zero-points on real data to map their range
Preventively pruning weights, always performed before each quantization phase
q: A team applies PTQ to INT8 and uses a sample of real data for calibration. What is this calibration for?

explain: QAT is indicated when PTQ degrades accuracy too much (typical at low bit-widths like INT8/INT4): by simulating quantization in training, the model learns weights robust to quantization error.
options: When wanting to avoid any additional retraining of the final model in production
Only for models already compressed to FP16 and ready for deployment on mobile hardware
When the training budget is zero but maximum accuracy is still needed
When PTQ degrades accuracy too much and a further training cycle can be afforded
q: In which situation is quantization-aware training (QAT) preferable to PTQ alone?

explain: Latency is the time per single request (critical for interactive chat), throughput is the number of requests completed per unit of time (critical for offline batches).
options: Latency is the time per single request, throughput the requests served per unit of time
They are interchangeable synonyms indicating the same quantity always measured in production
Latency only measures the training phase while throughput only measures the storage used
Throughput always equals the mathematical inverse of the perplexity of the model itself
q: In an LLM production tradeoff, what is the difference between latency and throughput?

explain: A reliable A/B test requires a sufficient sample and a significance test: differences on few samples can be pure statistical noise.
options: It suffices to compare arithmetic means computed on a sample of about 20 requests
An adequate sample and a significance test ruling out mere statistical noise are needed
Significance is only achieved by splitting traffic in a fixed 90-to-10 ratio
Statistical tests are entirely useless when evaluating modern large language models in production
q: Model B scores slightly higher than model A on 30 prompts. Why does a careful engineer not immediately declare B the winner?

explain: If traffic is not randomly assigned (e.g., premium users on one model and free users on the other), the comparison is distorted: the different users, not the models, explain the difference.
options: Using two completely different metrics to evaluate the two models being compared
Versioning both models with identical tags so as to confuse their inference logs
Assigning traffic non-randomly, for example premium users to A and free users to B
Monitoring only the latency of both models without ever comparing their generative quality
q: Which error introduces traffic bias in an A/B test between two LLMs?

explain: With c=10 and r=12 we have c < r, so BP = exp(1 - 12/10) = exp(-0.2) ≈ 0.82: a moderate penalty for a candidate about 17% shorter.
options: 1, because the brevity penalty never applies to candidates shorter than the reference
0, because the brevity penalty zeroes the score below the reference length
Exactly 0.5 by definition, whatever the candidate and reference lengths used
About 0.82, i.e. exp(1 - 12/10), because the candidate is shorter than the reference
q: In the BLEU formula, a candidate of length c=10 tokens has an effective reference length r=12 tokens. What is the brevity penalty?

explain: The candidate has 6 unigrams; 5 appear in the reference (only 'sat' is missing): precision = 5/6 ≈ 0.83, before applying brevity penalty and geometric mean.
options: 5/6, because 5 of the candidate's 6 unigrams also appear in the reference
6/6, because candidate and reference have the same overall meaning
4/6, because determiners must never be counted in precision
1/6, because only the differing word carries truly useful information
q: Candidate: 'The cat sat on the mat'. Reference: 'The cat is on the mat'. What is the unigram precision (BLEU-1 without brevity penalty)?

explain: The reference has 5 unigrams; the candidate captures 4 (only 'cat' is missing): recall = 4/5 = 0.80. Precision is also 4/5 because the candidate has 5 tokens.
options: 3/5, equal to the candidate precision computed by dividing by its 5 total tokens
4/5 = 0.80, because 4 of the reference's 5 unigrams are captured by the candidate
3/4 = 0.75, dividing the candidate's tokens by the given reference's total tokens
Full 1.0, because the overall meaning of the sentence is perfectly preserved
q: Reference: 'the cat sleeps on the couch' (5 tokens). Candidate: 'the dog sleeps on the couch' (5 tokens). What is ROUGE-1 recall?

explain: On Hopper/Ada/Blackwell, FP8 offers a good accuracy-speed tradeoff for transformers; INT8 gives greater compression but requires careful calibration, FP16 is the safest fallback.
options: Always using FP32 on every layer to get maximum inference speed
Going directly to INT4 on the whole model without any preliminary accuracy evaluation
Use FP8 on TensorRT with FP16 fallback, calibrated INT8 only for top compression
Avoiding any quantization because transformer models do not support it in any case
q: A team must serve an LLM on Hopper GPUs with TensorRT, reducing memory and latency with minimal accuracy loss. Which quantization strategy is most sensible?

explain: MMLU tests multitask multiple-choice knowledge and understanding, HELM holistically evaluates accuracy, robustness, fairness and efficiency: they are general capability benchmarks, complementary to generation metrics like BLEU/ROUGE.
options: Two n-gram precision metrics designed exclusively for machine translation
Two structured pruning techniques applied to large language model layers
Two quantization-aware training frameworks integrated into TensorRT and NVIDIA ModelOpt for deployment
Two general benchmark suites: MMLU for multitask knowledge, HELM for holistic evaluation
q: What are MMLU and HELM in the context of LLM evaluation?

explain: Hallucinations are fluent but false statements; RAG grounds the model in retrieved documents, reducing them, and evaluation must include human factuality because BLEU/ROUGE do not measure it.
options: Hallucinations motivate RAG and factual-correctness evaluation beyond BLEU and ROUGE
Hallucinations are fully eliminated by increasing the BLEU metric's brevity penalty
RAG increases model hallucinations but still improves the ROUGE score obtained
Automatic metrics always detect every hallucination with no need for humans
q: What is the link between hallucination, RAG and the limits of automatic metrics?

explain: A high temperature softens the teacher's soft labels, revealing inter-class relationships (dark knowledge); the loss combines cross-entropy on true labels and divergence toward soft targets.
options: Temperature controls the physical heat dissipated by the GPU during training
High T softens soft targets across classes and the loss combines cross-entropy and divergence
Distillation uses only hard labels and never uses any temperature
Distillation requires teacher and student with the same size and architecture
q: In knowledge distillation, what role do temperature (T) and the composite loss play?

explain: Magnitude pruning removes weights with the smallest absolute value; after pruning, fine-tuning is almost always needed to recover lost accuracy.
options: It removes weights with the largest absolute value because they dominate the model's final output too much
It randomly removes entire training datasets to lighten the total computational load
It removes weights with the smallest absolute value and is followed by fine-tuning to recover accuracy
It never requires any recovery or retraining after pruning the weights
q: What does magnitude pruning do and which step normally follows?

explain: Simultaneous 50/50 traffic with random assignment guarantees a fair comparison; simultaneous deployment controls temporal effects and randomization eliminates selection bias.
options: Launching the two models in different weeks to compare their historical usage trends
Routing all traffic to the new model immediately without keeping the old one active
Using different prompts for each model so as to cover the most scenarios
Serving both models together with random 50/50 traffic on the same prompts
q: To fairly compare two versions of an LLM in production while avoiding temporal and selection bias, which A/B test design is recommended?

explain: Flat metrics but growing negative feedback suggest semantic drift or out-of-distribution queries: query logging, metric recalibration with human judgments, and possible updates to data or retriever are needed.
options: Query drift relative to training invisible to BLEU/ROUGE: analysis and human judgments are needed
Simply increasing the metric's brevity penalty to penalize wrong answers
Further quantizing the model to INT4 to speed up generation of the answers given in production
Disabling monitoring because stable metrics guarantee adequate quality
q: After deploying a RAG assistant, BLEU and ROUGE stay stable but user complaints about irrelevant answers grow. What is the most likely diagnosis and the next step?

explain: BLEU is the standard lexical metric for machine translation because it measures the precision of the candidate's n-grams against the references.
options: ROUGE-L, because translation requires recall on the longest common subsequence
BLEU, because it measures the precision of the candidate's n-grams on the references
Perplexity, because translation needs no reference text
Average latency, because speed is the only criterion for a translator
q: A team must evaluate an English-to-Italian machine translation system with available human references. Which lexical metric is the most natural choice?

explain: Perplexity is computed from the probabilities the model assigns to the text, so it requires no human reference and is ideal for intrinsic fluency evaluation.
options: ROUGE-2, which compares the candidate's bigrams with a reference summary
BLEU with brevity penalty, which requires at least one parallel human reference
Perplexity, which uses only the model's probabilities and requires no references
Exact match, which checks identity between output and expected answer word by word
q: Which metric allows evaluating a model's fluency without any reference text?

explain: F1 is the harmonic mean of precision and recall: it penalizes cases where one of the two is low, unlike the arithmetic mean which would hide them.
options: The harmonic mean of precision and recall, which penalizes imbalance between the two
The arithmetic mean of accuracy and perplexity computed on the test set
The ratio of true positives to false negatives observed in production
The difference between the BLEU score and the ROUGE score on the same output
q: In classification, what is F1 defined as?

explain: BLEU measures n-gram precision with values between 0 and 1: a score of 0.85 indicates high lexical overlap with the reference.
options: Poor quality, because BLEU only rewards scores close to zero
High model uncertainty, equivalent to very high perplexity
High n-gram overlap between candidate and reference
Excellent recall on summaries, typical of the ROUGE metric
q: A translation system scores BLEU 0.85 on the test set. How is this interpreted?

explain: Without clipping, a candidate like 'the the the' would get perfect precision; the clipped count limits each n-gram to its occurrences in the reference and prevents this gaming.
options: To reward very short candidates repeating a single correct word
To clip counts to occurrences in the reference and prevent gaming
To remove from the computation all unigrams present in the reference
To convert precision into recall when references are multiple
q: Why does BLEU use modified (clipped) precision instead of plain precision?

explain: The candidate's bigrams are 5 (the-cat, cat-sat, sat-on, on-the, the-mat) and 3 appear in the reference (the-cat, on-the, the-mat): precision is 3/5 = 0.60.
options: 5/5 = 1.0, because the two sentences have identical overall meaning
4/5 = 0.80, also counting the bigram cat-sat as almost correct
3/5 = 0.60, i.e. 3 of the candidate's bigrams present in the reference
2/5 = 0.40, because determiners must never be counted in bigrams
q: Candidate: 'the cat sat on the mat'. Reference: 'the cat is on the mat'. What is the bigram precision?

explain: F-beta weights recall beta times more than precision: with beta = 2 (F2), false negatives cost more, which is right when missing a positive is serious, as in medical screening.
options: The average of BLEU and ROUGE computed on the same set of candidates
The ratio of inference latency to throughput in production
Perplexity measured only on the final tokens of each generated sequence
An F measure favoring recall, used when false negatives cost most
q: What does F2 (F-beta variant with beta = 2) measure and when is it appropriate?

explain: F1 = 2·P·R/(P+R) = 2·0.8·0.6/1.4 = 0.96/1.4 ≈ 0.69: closer to the smaller value, as typical for the harmonic mean.
options: About 0.70, i.e. the simple arithmetic mean of 0.8 and 0.6
About 0.48, i.e. the direct product of precision and recall
About 1.40, i.e. the sum of precision and recall on the test set
q: A classifier has precision 0.8 and recall 0.6 on the positive class. What is F1?

explain: The reference has 6 unigrams and the candidate captures 4 (the, dog, in, park): ROUGE-1 recall = 4/6 ≈ 0.67.
options: 5/6 ≈ 0.83, because almost all reference tokens are covered
4/6 ≈ 0.67, i.e. 4 of the reference's unigrams captured out of 6
4/5 = 0.80, dividing by the candidate's tokens instead of the reference's
1.0, because the two sentences describe the same park scene
q: Reference: 'the dog barks loudly in the park' (6 tokens). Candidate: 'the dog runs in the park' (5 tokens). What is ROUGE-1 recall?

explain: Perplexity = exp of the average negative log-likelihood: exp(1.5) ≈ 4.48, so the model is on average uncertain among about 4-5 tokens.
options: 1.5, because perplexity always equals the average loss
About 2.72, i.e. Euler's constant raised to the halved loss
About 4.48, i.e. exp(1.5) of the average negative log-likelihood
About 0.22, i.e. the inverse of the average negative log-likelihood
q: A model has average negative log-likelihood of 1.5 on the test set. What is the perplexity?

explain: Overlap of 4 tokens out of 4 in the candidate (precision 1.0) and out of 5 in the reference (recall 0.8): token-level F1 = 2·1·0.8/1.8 ≈ 0.89.
options: About 0.89, with precision 1.0 on the candidate and recall 0.80 on the reference
Full 1.0, because exact match and F1 always coincide in QA
0.0, because the two sentences have different word order
About 0.50, i.e. the average of the candidate and reference lengths
q: Reference: 'Canberra is the Australian capital'. Candidate: 'the capital is Canberra'. What is the token-level F1?

explain: Macro-average averages per-class F1 with equal weight: (0.9+0.6+0.3)/3 = 0.60, without being dominated by frequent classes.
options: 0.90, i.e. the best class's F1 representing the whole model
0.60, i.e. the unweighted average of the three class F1s
0.30, i.e. the worst class's F1 zeroing out the others
0.75, i.e. the average of the best and worst classes
q: Three classes have F1 of 0.9, 0.6 and 0.3. What is the macro-F1?

explain: Faithfulness measures whether the answer is grounded in the retrieved context; an invented detail is a hallucination.
options: Faithfulness, because the claim is not supported by the retrieved context
Fluency, because the sentence contains an obvious grammatical error
Perplexity, because the answer is too predictable
Context recall, because a document on dosage is missing
q: A RAG system answers: 'Drug X is approved for children under 5', but the retrieved passages only discuss adult use and never mention children. Which evaluation metric flags the problem?

explain: Answer relevance compares answer and question: an off-topic answer scores low even if factual.
options: Context precision, because the retrieved documents are too long
Answer relevance, because the answer does not address the question asked
Faithfulness, because the answer correctly cites the manual
Answer correctness, because the answer is too short
q: A user asks: 'How can I reset my router password?'. The RAG system retrieves the correct manual but answers with the manufacturer's company history. Which metric is low?

explain: The relevant document is present (recall ok) but buried among many irrelevant ones, so precision is low.
options: High context recall but low answer correctness
High faithfulness but low answer relevance
Low context precision but high context recall
High context relevance but low verbosity
q: For the question 'What is the capital of Australia?' retrieval returns 5 passages: 4 about tourism in Sydney and 1 citing Canberra as the capital. How is this retrieval described?
source: Adattata da Udemy – practice test NCA-GENL

explain: Answer correctness measures factual correspondence with the ground truth, unlike metrics based only on context or question.
options: Context relevance, which compares question and retrieved passages
Faithfulness, which compares answer and retrieved context
Answer relevance, which compares question and generated answer
Answer correctness, which compares generated answer and ground truth
q: A team evaluates a RAG system on 100 questions with reference (ground truth) answers. Which metric measures how well generated answers match the expected answers?

explain: Precision evaluates the quality of the ranking obtained, recall evaluates the coverage of all available relevant material.
options: Context precision rates top passages' relevance; context recall rates coverage of all relevant ones
Context precision measures retrieval speed, context recall measures token cost
Context precision compares answer and question, context recall compares answer and ground truth in this RAG setup
Context precision requires a human judge, context recall requires only perplexity

explain: Verbosity bias leads the LLM judge to mistake a longer answer for a better answer.
options: Position bias, because it prefers the first answer shown
Verbosity bias, because it rewards length instead of quality
Self-preference bias, because it prefers its own writing style
Recency bias, because it rewards the most recent information
q: An LLM-based automatic evaluator systematically assigns higher scores to verbose answers, even when they say the same things as concise answers. Which bias does it show?

explain: Sensitivity to order indicates position bias; balanced presentations in both orders neutralize it.
options: By increasing the generator's temperature for more variety
By computing the perplexity of both answers on the judge model
By averaging judgments with swapped order or randomizing position in comparisons
By replacing the LLM judge with the BLEU metric
q: In an LLM-judge evaluation, the same model judges two answers A and B: when A is presented first, A wins; when the order is reversed, B wins. How is this effect corrected?

explain: Self-preference bias is mitigated by separating generator and judge or hiding which answer comes from whom.
options: Using only very short answers to hide style
Lowering the judge's temperature to zero to make its verdicts fully deterministic
Measuring context recall instead of quality
Using a different judge model or hiding each answer's origin
q: An LLM judge evaluates answers generated by the same model acting as judge and prefers them over other models' answers at equal quality. Which remedy reduces this problem?

explain: BLEU and ROUGE measure word and n-gram overlap between generated text and reference.
options: Lexical overlap metrics like BLEU and ROUGE
Context-based faithfulness metrics
Ranking metrics like context precision
Inter-annotator agreement measures
q: A team compares a generated answer with a reference answer and counts how many n-grams overlap. Which metric family does this approach belong to?

explain: Lower perplexity indicates better language modeling, but does not guarantee answers faithful to the retrieved context.

Fluency on the domain improved, but perplexity says nothing about context grounding
Faithfulness has improved because perplexity directly measures hallucinations
Context recall has increased because retrieval finds more relevant documents
q: A language model scores perplexity 15 on a test corpus and, after domain adaptation, drops to 8 on the same test. What does this change indicate and what is its limitation for a RAG system?

explain: High agreement shows the task is well-defined and labels are stable; if low, guidelines must be revised.

To train the retriever to rank documents better
To verify that guidelines are clear and labels are reliable
To automatically compute the generator model's perplexity
q: Two human annotators label 100 RAG answers as 'faithful' or 'not faithful' to the context. Why is inter-annotator agreement computed before using these labels?

explain: If the answer is faithful to the context but wrong against the ground truth, the problem is upstream in retrieval.
options: The generator invents facts that are nowhere present in any of the retrieved passages
The LLM judge suffers from obvious verbosity bias
The ROUGE metric is configured with the wrong n-gram
Wrong but coherent passages retrieved, then faithfully summarized
